newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch call money rates rise ahead of quota expiry.
newsitem.headline: Dutch call money rates rise ahead of quota expiry.

text.p: Dutch call money rates surged on Wednesday as banks cleared their books ahead of next week's expiry of the three month credit quota. Dealers said call was also up because the Dutch government was in need of liquidity.
Call money rates were bid at 3.12 to 3.18 percent in late afternoon after touching a day's high of 3.25 percent earlier versus 3.00 percent bid on Tuesday.
The credit quota is a three-monthly limit on the amount banks can borrow through the central bank's regular credit facilities at the secured loans rate, the lowest available.
The current quota expires on Friday, April 18.
The secured loans rate was raised on March 10 to 2.50 percent from 2.00 percent.
"Some banks have used too much of their quota and they are taking in extra liquidity in the money market just to be on the safe side," said one dealer.
He added banks were early in anticipating the expiry.
Another dealer said he hoped call rates would not rise any further ahead of the expiry.
"But it is possible, because not only the expiry but also the government's search for liquidity is putting upward pressure on call money rates," he said.
The dealer added that the government was awaiting income from tax payments, but that there was currently a deficiency.
The Dutch central bank set today's overnight AIBOR at 3.23 percent from 3.13 percent on Tuesday as call had been moving up in the money market.
Dealers noted little business in Dutch Treasury Certificates (DTCs), the short term borrowing programme of the Dutch government.
The May programme was priced at 3.13 percent, the new June programme at 3.15 percent and the December programme at 3.25 percent.
"This is not a bad price if you look at today's one-month and two month deposits," said one dealer, but he said that there were only few buyers because some were hoping for even higher returns.
"The new programme should bring in 7.5 billion guilders and there is much to go," he said.
